sections.heading: Dancing on Helicon
sections.translation:
Let us begin our song with the Muses, goddesses of song,
who live on Helicon, the great and sacred mountain.
On soft feet they dance around the violet-dark spring
and the altar of mighty Zeus, the son of Cronus.
After washing their tender skin in the river Permessus,
or the Horse’s Spring, or the sacred river Olmeius,
they form lovely, graceful dances high on Helicon,
their feet moving with force.
sections.summary: The Muses wash in sacred waters and dance on Mount Helicon.

cards.label: Muses
cards.general: Goddesses who inspire song and poetry.
cards.here: They dance on their sacred mountain.

cards.label: Helicon
cards.general: A mountain in Greece associated with the Muses.
cards.here: Its springs and heights are places where they wash and dance.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the Greek gods.
cards.here: The Muses dance around his altar.

cards.label: Cronus
cards.general: A god of the older generation, called the Titans.
cards.here: He is named as Zeus’s father.

cards.label: Altar
cards.general: A structure where people make offerings to a god.
cards.here: This altar belongs to Zeus.

cards.label: Permessus
cards.general: A river near Mount Helicon.
cards.here: One of the waters where the Muses bathe.

cards.label: Horse’s Spring
cards.general: A spring on Helicon, also called Hippocrene.
cards.here: Another bathing place for the Muses.

cards.label: Olmeius
cards.general: A river near Mount Helicon.
cards.here: Hesiod calls its waters sacred.

sections.heading: A Song Full of Gods
sections.summary: Hidden in mist, the Muses travel at night and sing about the gods.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods and father of Athena.
cards.here: He carries the aegis and begins the list of gods.

cards.label: Aegis
cards.general: A divine protective object, pictured as a shield or cloak.
cards.here: Carrying it marks Zeus’s power.

cards.label: Hera
cards.general: Zeus’s wife and queen of the gods.
cards.here: She is linked with Argos and wears golden sandals.

cards.label: Argos
cards.general: A Greek city and surrounding region where Hera was worshipped.
cards.here: Hesiod calls Hera “of Argos.”

cards.label: Athena
cards.general: Zeus’s daughter, a goddess of wisdom, crafts, and warfare.
cards.here: She is described as bright-eyed.

cards.label: Apollo
cards.general: A god associated with music, prophecy, and archery.
cards.here: He is called shining, translating the name Phoebus.

cards.label: Artemis
cards.general: A goddess of hunting and Apollo’s sister.
cards.here: She showers arrows.

cards.label: Poseidon
cards.general: A god of the sea and earthquakes.
cards.here: He holds the earth and shakes it.

cards.label: Themis
cards.general: A goddess of justice and rightful order.
cards.here: The Muses sing of her with honor.

cards.label: Aphrodite
cards.general: The goddess of love and desire.
cards.here: Hesiod draws attention to her eyes or lashes.

cards.label: Hebe
cards.general: The goddess of youth.
cards.here: She wears a golden crown.

cards.label: Dione
cards.general: A goddess whose name is closely related to Zeus’s.
cards.here: She is praised as beautiful.

cards.label: Leto
cards.general: The mother of Apollo and Artemis.
cards.here: She is among the gods praised in the song.

cards.label: Iapetus
cards.general: One of the Titans, the older generation of gods.
cards.here: He appears alongside Leto and Cronus.

cards.label: Cronus
cards.general: A Titan and Zeus’s father.
cards.here: He is described as crafty in his planning.

cards.label: Eos
cards.general: Dawn imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is named alongside the Sun and Moon.

cards.label: Helios
cards.general: The Sun imagined as a god.
cards.here: Hesiod calls him great.

cards.label: Selene
cards.general: The Moon imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is described as bright.

cards.label: Gaia
cards.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is included among the eternal gods.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river believed to flow around the world.
cards.here: He is praised as great.

cards.label: Night
cards.general: Night imagined as a goddess, called Nyx in Greek.
cards.here: She is described as black.

cards.label: Immortal
cards.general: Able to live forever.
cards.here: The song praises the whole family of everlasting gods.

sections.heading: The Muses Give Hesiod a Voice
sections.translation:
These were the goddesses who once taught Hesiod beautiful song
while he tended lambs below sacred Helicon.
This is what they said to me first—
the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who carries the aegis:
“Shepherds who live out in the fields, shameful creatures, nothing but bellies!
We know how to tell many lies that sound like the truth;
and we know, when we choose, how to speak the truth.”
So spoke great Zeus’s daughters, their words clear and sure.
They plucked a branch from a flourishing laurel tree
and gave it to me as a staff—a wonderful sight.
Then they breathed a divine voice into me,
so I could sing of things to come and things long past.
They told me to praise the family of blessed gods who live forever,
and always to sing of the Muses themselves, first and last.
sections.summary: The Muses speak sharply to Hesiod, then give him a staff and the power to sing about the gods.

cards.label: Hesiod
cards.general: The Greek poet speaking in this poem.
cards.here: He says the Muses taught him while he was tending lambs.

cards.label: Muses
cards.general: Goddesses who inspire poetry and song.
cards.here: They give Hesiod his poetic voice and tell him what to sing.

cards.label: Helicon
cards.general: A sacred mountain in Greece.
cards.here: Hesiod meets the Muses below it.

cards.label: Olympus
cards.general: The mountain home of the gods.
cards.here: Calling the Muses “of Olympus” connects them with the divine household.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods.
cards.here: He is the Muses’ father and carries the divine aegis.

cards.label: Nothing but bellies
cards.general: An insult suggesting that someone cares only about food.
cards.here: The Muses use it to mock the shepherds.

cards.label: Laurel staff
cards.general: A long stick made from a laurel tree, which has glossy evergreen leaves.
cards.here: The Muses give it to Hesiod as a sign of his new authority as a singer.

cards.label: Divine
cards.general: Coming from or belonging to the gods.
cards.here: Hesiod’s new singing voice comes from the Muses.

sections.heading: A Song That Fills Olympus
sections.translation:
But why am I talking like this about oak or rock?
Come, let us begin with the Muses.
Inside Olympus, the mountain home of the gods,
their songs delight the great mind of Zeus their father.
Their voices join as they tell of what is,
what will be, and what was before.
Sweet song flows tirelessly from their mouths.
Their father Zeus’s halls laugh with joy—
Zeus whose thunder booms—as the goddesses’ lily-delicate voices spread.
The peak of snowy Olympus echoes,
and so do the homes of the immortal gods.
Sending out their deathless voices,
they first sing in praise of the gods’ honored family from the beginning:
those born to Gaia the Earth and wide Uranus the Sky,
and the gods descended from them, the givers of good things.
Next they sing of Zeus, father of gods and humans,
at both the beginning and the end of their song:
how far he surpasses the gods, how greatest he is in power.
Then they sing of humankind and the mighty Giants,
those powerful beings of the ancient divine world.
So the Muses of Olympus, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus,
delight their father’s mind inside Olympus.
sections.summary: The Muses fill Olympus with song about the gods’ beginnings, Zeus’s power, humans, and Giants.

cards.label: Oak or rock
cards.general: An old expression whose exact meaning here is uncertain.
cards.here: Hesiod uses it as he breaks off his personal story and returns to the Muses.

cards.label: Muses
cards.general: Goddesses of song and poetry.
cards.here: Their united voices delight Zeus and make Olympus echo.

cards.label: Olympus
cards.general: The mountain home of the gods.
cards.here: Its snowy peak and divine halls ring with the Muses’ song.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods and the Muses’ father.
cards.here: Their song celebrates his supreme power.

cards.label: Lily-delicate
cards.general: A comparison with a lily flower, suggesting delicacy and beauty.
cards.here: Hesiod uses the flower image to describe the goddesses’ voices.

cards.label: Gaia
cards.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She and Uranus are parents of an early generation of gods.

cards.label: Uranus
cards.general: The Sky imagined as a god.
cards.here: With Gaia, he fathers the gods whose family history the Muses sing.

cards.label: Giants
cards.general: A race of powerful beings in Greek myth.
cards.here: They are a separate subject of the Muses’ song, alongside humankind.

cards.label: Aegis
cards.general: A divine shield or protective cloak.
cards.here: It identifies Zeus as the powerful father of the Muses.

sections.heading: Nine Daughters of Memory
sections.translation:
In Pieria, a region near Olympus, Mnemosyne—Memory herself,
who rules the hills of Eleuther—slept with their father,
Zeus the son of Cronus, and gave birth to the Muses:
forgetfulness of troubles, a rest from worries.
For nine nights Zeus, wise in planning, lay with her,
climbing into her sacred bed far from the other gods.
When a year had passed and the seasons had turned,
as the months waned and many days completed their course,
she gave birth to nine daughters, all of one mind.
Song fills their hearts, and their spirits are free from care.
She bore them a little way below the highest peak of snowy Olympus.
sections.summary: Memory and Zeus have nine daughters, the Muses, whose songs bring relief from worry.

cards.label: Pieria
cards.general: A region near Mount Olympus associated with the Muses.
cards.here: It is the setting for their birth.

cards.label: Mnemosyne
cards.general: The goddess of memory; her name means “Memory.”
cards.here: She is the mother of the nine Muses.

cards.label: Eleuther
cards.general: A place or hill whose exact identification is uncertain.
cards.here: Mnemosyne rules its hills.

cards.label: Zeus, son of Cronus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods, born to the older god Cronus.
cards.here: He spends nine nights with Mnemosyne and fathers the Muses.

cards.label: Muses
cards.general: Nine goddesses who inspire poetry and song.
cards.here: They share one purpose, love song, and bring relief from troubles.

cards.label: Olympus
cards.general: The mountain home of the gods.
cards.here: The Muses are born near its highest snowy peak.

uncertainties: In line 13, Athena’s eye epithet can suggest brightness, gray coloring, or an association with owls. “Bright-eyed” keeps its visual force without choosing a precise color.
In line 16, Aphrodite’s epithet is interpreted in several ways, including curved eyelids, curling lashes, or an alluring glance. “Curling lashes” is one possible reading.
The exact force of “oak or rock” in line 35 is disputed. The translation preserves the image; in context it marks Hesiod’s return from his personal story to the Muses.
The place called Eleuther in line 54 cannot be identified securely.
